history.heading: Ancient and early Christian Ireland
paragraphs: Ireland has been inhabited for over 10,000 years. Neolithic farmers built monumental tombs such as Newgrange, older than the pyramids of Giza. Celtic culture and the Irish language developed during the Iron Age, with society organised into many small kingdoms.

Saint Patrick and other missionaries brought Christianity in the 5th century. Irish monasteries became centres of learning during the early Middle Ages, producing illuminated manuscripts such as the Book of Kells, and Irish monks spread Christianity across Europe. Vikings raided from the late 8th century and founded towns including Dublin.

history.heading: English rule
paragraphs: Anglo-Norman invaders arrived in 1169, beginning centuries of English involvement. In the 16th and 17th centuries, England conquered the whole island and confiscated land, settling Protestant colonists, especially in Ulster. Penal laws discriminated against the Catholic majority. The 1798 rebellion failed, and the 1800 Act of Union made Ireland part of the United Kingdom.
The Great Famine of 1845–1852, caused by potato blight and worsened by British policy, killed about a million people and forced another million to emigrate, beginning a long decline in population.

history.heading: Independence
paragraphs: The Easter Rising of 1916 was quickly suppressed, but the execution of its leaders boosted support for independence. After the War of Independence (1919–21), the Anglo-Irish Treaty created the Irish Free State, while six northeastern counties remained in the UK as Northern Ireland. A civil war followed over the treaty.
Ireland became a republic in 1949. In Northern Ireland, the Troubles (1968–1998) killed over 3,500 people, until the Good Friday Agreement of 1998 brought peace.

history.heading: Modern Ireland
paragraphs: Ireland joined the European Economic Community in 1973. From the 1990s the "Celtic Tiger" economy transformed it into one of Europe's richest countries, though it suffered a severe banking crisis in 2008. Society changed rapidly, with referendums legalising same-sex marriage in 2015 and abortion in 2018.

culture.heading: Language and literature
paragraphs: Irish (Gaelic) is the national and first official language, though English is spoken by nearly everyone; Irish is spoken as a community language in Gaeltacht areas. Ireland has a remarkable literary tradition, with writers such as Jonathan Swift, Oscar Wilde, James Joyce, Samuel Beckett and four Nobel laureates in literature, including W. B. Yeats and Seamus Heaney.
Most people are Catholic by tradition, though church attendance has fallen sharply.

culture.heading: Music, sport and celebration
paragraphs: Traditional Irish music and dance are popular worldwide, and Ireland has produced artists such as U2, Van Morrison, Sinéad O'Connor and Enya. Saint Patrick's Day on 17 March is celebrated around the world by the large Irish diaspora.

Gaelic games, hurling and Gaelic football, are the most popular sports, organised by the amateur Gaelic Athletic Association. Rugby is played on an all-island basis. The pub is central to social life, and Guinness stout is famous worldwide.

politics.heading: Parliamentary republic
paragraphs: Ireland is a parliamentary republic. The Taoiseach (prime minister) leads the government, responsible to the Dáil, the lower house of the Oireachtas (parliament). The president is directly elected for seven years with a mainly ceremonial role.

Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael, the two parties that emerged from the civil war, have dominated politics and govern together; Sinn Féin has become a major force. Ireland is an EU member and militarily neutral, not a member of NATO.

economy.heading: A global hub
paragraphs: Ireland has one of the highest GDPs per person in the world, partly because many multinational companies, especially US tech and pharmaceutical firms such as Apple, Google, Meta, Pfizer and Intel, have their European headquarters there, attracted by its low corporate tax rate, English-speaking workforce and EU membership.

Agriculture, especially beef and dairy, food and drink, tourism and financial services are also important. The currency is the euro. A severe housing shortage and high rents are major challenges, and the economy depends heavily on a few large foreign firms.
